Strategy & Business — Business Models

Revenue Models

Which way of charging fits this product, and what does each trade off? A near-expert treatment: the mechanism behind the mechanism, the arithmetic that decides it, the seams where it breaks, and the disagreements the field has not settled.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On 3 February 2026, in a glass-walled room on the fourth floor of an office block off Baner Road in Pune, Nandita Kulkarni put a single sheet of paper in front of her chief financial officer and waited. Kulkarni was chief product officer of Dhanika Labs, a four-year-old company whose software read loan files — sanction letters, bank statements, GST returns, title documents — and produced a structured credit summary for the underwriters of mid-market non-banking financial companies. Dhanika had 240 customer accounts, 6,400 paid seats, and charged ₹1,250 per seat per month. That was ₹9.60 crore of annual recurring revenue, growing at 60 percent, and every investor deck the company had ever written had described the model in the same three words: per-seat subscription.

The sheet of paper ranked Dhanika's seats into ten equal groups by how many document sets each one processed in a month. The first group averaged eight. The tenth averaged six hundred and fifteen. At the company's blended inference and retrieval cost of ₹3.60 per document set — a number Tomás Ferreira, Dhanika's machine-learning infrastructure lead in Lisbon, had spent six weeks reconstructing from three cloud bills and a vector-store invoice — the top tenth of seats cost ₹2,214 a month to serve against a price of ₹1,250. Six hundred and forty seats, the company's most enthusiastic and most reference-able users, were losing ₹964 each, every month, and their usage was compounding at six percent a month. Dhanika's blended gross margin was 61 percent and falling roughly a point a quarter, entirely because its best customers were succeeding.

Kulkarni's problem was not that the price was too low. The price was fine for seven of the ten deciles. Her problem was that a flat per-seat charge is an implicit promise to absorb unlimited consumption, and Dhanika had made that promise in 2022 when a document set cost the company eleven paise to process because the product was mostly regular expressions and a rules engine. The mechanism had outlived the cost structure it was designed around. She had until the Series B close in June to propose something else, and the something else would have to be sold back to 240 customers who had signed contracts on the old basis.

Two weeks later and twelve hundred kilometres north, Kabir Sethi was looking at a different sheet of paper with the same shape of problem underneath it. Sethi had co-founded Dravid Freight Exchange in 2019; it matched shippers — cement plants, FMCG distributors, e-commerce fulfilment centres — with the owners of India's enormous, fragmented long-haul trucking fleet. In the financial year just ending, Dravid had handled ₹1,420 crore of freight across 3.1 lakh trips and taken a commission of 8.2 percent, which produced ₹116.4 crore of revenue. After carrier incentives (2.1 percent of freight value), collections and payment costs (0.4 percent), insurance and claims (0.6 percent) and the cost of the operations desk that babysat every load (1.3 percent), the contribution left over was 3.8 percent of freight value, or ₹54 crore. Corporate overhead was ₹71 crore. The company lost ₹17 crore at the EBITDA line and had done so, in varying amounts, every year of its existence.

What Wei Lin Tan, Dravid's Singapore-based data scientist, had put in front of Sethi was not a cost line. It was a retention curve of a kind Sethi had never asked for. Of shipper–carrier pairs that Dravid introduced to each other and that subsequently ran the same lane again, 27 percent of those repeat trips happened off the platform within ninety days. The two parties met on Dravid, discovered that they liked each other, exchanged phone numbers, and from the fourth or fifth load onward settled directly over UPI. Dravid's commission was, in the most literal sense, a tax on an introduction that only had to be made once.

Sethi's board wanted the take rate raised to nine percent. Tan's data implied that raising it would accelerate the leak. The question in front of Sethi was not what number to charge. It was whether a commission was the right mechanism at all for a business whose core service — the match — was consumed once and then owned by the customer forever.

Kulkarni was being asked to change what she charged for. Sethi was being asked to change who he was charging and why. Both had been told they had a pricing problem. Neither did.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

A revenue model is the mechanism by which a firm converts value it has created into cash it actually collects. It specifies four things: who pays, what unit they are billed against, how often the charge repeats, and whether the amount scales with the value the customer receives. It is the capture half of a business model; the creation half — value proposition, channel, cost structure — is a separate design problem that the revenue model cannot rescue. Price is a number set inside a mechanism. The mechanism is the thing under discussion here.

The vocabulary arrived by accretion rather than by invention. In 2001, Peter Weill and Michael Vitale at MIT's Center for Information Systems Research published a taxonomy of "atomic business models" observed in early e-commerce, in which the revenue mechanism appeared as one axis along which otherwise similar ventures differed. Alexander Osterwalder's Business Model Canvas, formalised in his 2004 doctoral work and popularised by Business Model Generation in 2010, gave "Revenue Streams" a box on the page opposite "Cost Structure", and in doing so made a claim that was not obvious at the time: that how you charge is a design decision made deliberately, not a consequence that falls out of the product once it exists. Around the same time, the economics of two-sided markets — Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole's 2003 paper being the canonical reference — established something sharper still: that in platform businesses, the structure of prices across the two sides can matter more than the level, because a platform can be profitable at prices that would look suicidal on either side taken alone.

Three schools now argue about what follows from this, and the disagreement is real rather than definitional. It is worth stating each as a proposition its adherents would sign and its opponents would not.

The value-metric school holds that the correct revenue model is derived from the unit in which the customer experiences value, and that everything else is a distortion introduced by sales convenience or accounting habit. A practitioner in this school will sign: "If the customer's benefit doubles, the bill should roughly double, and if it does not, one of us is being defrauded." They will not sign: "A flat annual fee is acceptable so long as it is easy to forecast." Their strongest evidence is the observed expansion behaviour of consumption-priced software, where net revenue retention routinely exceeds 120 percent without any sales effort at all, because the meter simply runs.

The budget-line school holds that the correct revenue model is derived from the buyer's procurement reality — what line item the spending can sit on, what approval it requires, what variance the buyer's own budget can absorb. They will sign: "A model the customer cannot forecast is a model the customer will eventually cap, cancel or route around, however well it tracks value." They will not sign: "The meter should run freely because that is what is fair." Their evidence is the long list of usage-priced vendors who watched a large account install a hard spend cap, a rate limiter, or a home-grown alternative for the expensive 10 percent of the workload.

The lock-in school — the least polite and, on the evidence, frequently the most predictive — holds that the revenue model's real job is to sit where the customer cannot get around it, and that value correlation and budget comfort are secondary to defensibility. They will sign: "A charge that can be disintermediated is not a revenue model, it is a finder's fee, and it will decay towards zero." They will not sign: "Take rate should be set at the level that maximises current gross profit." Their evidence is precisely Sethi's 27 percent leakage number, replicated across freight, home services, tutoring and wholesale in every market where the two matched parties can transact without the intermediary.

These three positions recommend genuinely different actions in Kulkarni's and Sethi's situations, and no synthesis reconciles them. The rest of this page works through the mechanics carefully enough that a reader can tell which school a given argument is coming from, which is the first step in refereeing a disagreement between two competent people who are each half right.

3. Mechanics in depth: what the archetype label leaves out

Every introductory treatment names six archetypes and stops. The six are worth naming once — subscription, transaction or usage, commission, advertising, licensing, and hardware margin — but the expert work begins with the properties the label conceals. The formal core: three equations that decide most arguments

Revenue models are not usually taught quantitatively, which is a mistake, because three simple decompositions settle a surprising share of practitioner disputes.

First, revenue identity by mechanism. For a subscription, revenue equals the number of paying units multiplied by the price per period: R = N × p. For a usage model, revenue equals customers multiplied by consumed quantity multiplied by unit price: R = N × q × p. For a commission model, revenue equals gross transaction value multiplied by take rate: R = GMV × t. The identities are trivial. What they reveal is which variable the company actually controls. Dhanika controls N and p but not q; its customers control q, and q is exactly what drives its cost. Dravid controls t but not GMV, and — this is the uncomfortable part — t and GMV are not independent, because raising t pushes GMV off the platform.

Second, contribution per account, not per company. The blended gross margin on a profit-and-loss statement is an average, and averages hide the only distribution that matters. Write contribution for an account as m = p − c·q, where c is the marginal cost of serving one unit of consumption. Under a flat price, expected contribution is p − c·E[q] — which is why Dhanika's finance team saw a perfectly respectable 61 percent — but the variance of q is doing all the damage. When usage is heavy-tailed, as it almost always is in software, the mean is a poor summary. Dhanika's decile table is the whole argument in one page, and it is reproduced as Table 2.

Third, the three-part tariff. The practitioner's standard answer to a heavy tail is not to abandon the subscription but to decompose the bill into three terms: a platform fee F per account per period, an included allowance A of consumption, and an overage rate r beyond it. The customer's bill is F + r · max(0, q − A). Each term does a distinct job. F buys forecastability for the buyer and cash predictability for the seller — it is the term the budget-line school insists on. A is set high enough that the great majority of accounts never see an overage line, which keeps procurement calm. r protects the margin floor in the tail — it is the term the value-metric school insists on. Setting A at roughly the 70th to 80th percentile of observed consumption is the conventional starting point, and it is conventional because it leaves seven or eight deciles feeling as though nothing has changed while capping the firm's exposure to the two that were bleeding it.

The second-order effects the equations imply but do not state

Four consequences follow from the mechanics and are routinely missed.

Selection. A revenue model chooses customers before marketing does. A flat price is, formally, an insurance contract in which the seller underwrites the buyer's consumption; like any insurance contract priced at the population mean, it attracts the buyers who expect to consume above it. Dhanika's most enthusiastic users did not become expensive by accident — the flat price selected for them. Conversely, a purely usage-priced product selects for light and intermittent users, and repels precisely the large committed accounts that make enterprise sales economics work. Neither pure form is neutral.

Behavioural feedback. Changing the mechanism changes customer behaviour, which changes the volumes the new model was projected on. Any forecast of a move to usage pricing that holds q constant is wrong by construction: heavy users will batch, filter, pre-screen and deduplicate. Kulkarni's team eventually assumed an 18 percent reduction in consumption in the top two deciles once a meter was visible, and this turned out to be the single most consequential assumption in the model — it reduced projected revenue, but it also reduced cost, and it improved margin in a way the naive model had not shown.

Internal incentives. The revenue model silently rewrites what the organisation optimises. Sales compensation attaches to whatever the mechanism makes countable. An advertising model pays product managers, through their metrics, to increase time spent; a usage model pays them to increase consumption, which can directly oppose the customer's own efficiency goals; a hardware model pays the channel for sell-in, not sell-through, and the difference shows up as unsold inventory eighteen months later.

Cash timing. Revenue recognition and cash collection are different calendars, and a change of mechanism moves them relative to each other. A one-time sale collects and recognises the same day. An annual prepaid subscription collects on day one and recognises over twelve months, producing deferred revenue — a liability that is also, in practice, free working capital. A marketplace that pays carriers in three days and collects from shippers in forty-five has negative float: it funds its own growth out of its own balance sheet, which is why fast-growing commission businesses so often need debt that their revenue growth appears not to justify.

4. When the framework applies, and when it actively misleads

There are also situations in which the archetype framework is not merely unhelpful but misleading, and an expert names them before applying it. First, when regulation has already removed the choice. A payments business in India cannot price merchant discount on UPI person-to-merchant transactions, because the rate is zero by statute; debating the revenue model as if it were a design space wastes the meeting. Second, when the real business is a balance sheet. A great many Indian "marketplaces" earn more from lending against their transaction data than from any commission, and classifying them by their commission line describes the smaller half of the company. Third, when revenue-model discussion is being used to avoid the prior question. A subscription laid over a product nobody wants converts a one-time disappointment into a recurring one; mechanism cannot manufacture willingness to pay. Fourth, when the company is early enough that its true revenue model is venture funding, and the mechanism it presents to customers is a hypothesis with a price attached rather than a business.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product firms and the internal transfer-pricing problem

Once a firm runs two revenue models, a question appears that no canvas anticipates: who owns the customer relationship, and at what price does one stream sell to the other? If Dhanika's document-extraction engine is licensed to a core-banking vendor at ₹6 per document while the direct seat business effectively charges ₹13 for the same work, the licensing team has been handed a mandate to undercut its own colleagues. Mature firms handle this with an explicit internal price and a channel-conflict policy, but the honest description of how most handle it is that the larger stream wins the argument and the smaller one is quietly starved. The organisational tell is a pricing committee whose membership is drawn from finance and sales but not from the product teams whose margin is being decided.

Two-sided markets: structure beats level

Rochet and Tirole's central result is that in a two-sided market, total volume depends on the price structure — how the total charge is split across the sides — and not only on the total. The side that is subsidised should be the one with higher price elasticity, lower multi-homing cost, or greater cross-side externality. Dravid has been charging effectively all of its fee to the shipper side through a freight-inclusive rate, on the theory that carriers are poor and price-sensitive. The theory is half right: carriers are price-sensitive, but they are also the side that multi-homes least willingly, because switching apps means retraining drivers. On that reading, the carrier side is where a recurring charge would stick, and the shipper side is where it should be shaved — the exact inverse of what Dravid does.

Regulated categories: the menu is set before the team sits down

In India the Reserve Bank of India's payment-aggregator framework governs whether a platform may touch customer funds at all; the digital lending guidelines cap first-loss default guarantees at five percent of a loan portfolio, which sets a hard ceiling on how much credit risk a platform can carry without a licence; IRDAI caps insurance commissions by product class; and the zero-MDR regime on UPI removed a transaction-fee model from an entire industry overnight. An expert treats the regulatory perimeter as an input to the revenue-model design, drawn before the archetypes are considered, and not as a compliance review conducted after the model has been chosen. The mid-level version of this mistake is a beautifully argued revenue model that requires a licence the company will not obtain for three years.

Hardware plus software: allocation, arbitrage and attach

When a device is bundled with a service, Ind AS 115 requires the transaction price to be allocated across distinct performance obligations at relative standalone selling prices — so a firm cannot simply declare that a ₹6,000 bundle is ₹3,000 of hardware and ₹3,000 of deferred service because that flatters the recurring-revenue narrative. Separately, any model that sells hardware below cost to seed a service creates an arbitrage: if the device is useful without the subscription, it will be bought, resold and unbundled. The console business solved this with platform-level technical lock and licensed content; most consumer hardware companies have no equivalent lock and discover the arbitrage through their own grey-market channel. The diagnostic question is blunt: what physically prevents a buyer from taking the subsidised hardware and never subscribing? If the answer is "we hope they will want to", the cross-subsidy is a discount, not a model.

AI-native products: the cost floor moves, and so does the seat

Two properties make AI-native revenue models genuinely new rather than a re-run of software-as-a-service. The first is that cost of goods sold is variable, material and falling — a firm that designs a margin structure around today's inference price is designing around a number that may halve within eighteen months, which argues for contract terms that let the seller keep some of that decline rather than passing all of it through. The second is that agentic products dissolve the seat. If one underwriter using Dhanika's product can do the work of four, the customer's seat count falls even as the value delivered rises, and a per-seat model converts the vendor's own success into revenue contraction. This is the strongest argument for consumption or outcome pricing in AI, and it is why the seat-versus-usage question is the live disagreement of the moment rather than a settled one.

Outcome pricing — charging per resolved ticket, per approved loan file, per successful collection — is the frontier case and deserves a caution. It transfers model risk from the buyer to the seller: the vendor is now paid only when the model performs, which means an unlucky quarter of model drift shows up directly in revenue, not merely in churn risk. Firms that adopt it successfully almost always keep a platform fee underneath it, for exactly the reason the three-part tariff exists.

6. Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the value metric must be forecastable by the customer, not merely correlated with value. The competent practitioner finds the unit that best tracks benefit and stops there. The expert asks a second question — can the buyer predict next quarter's bill within about fifteen percent without doing any work? A metric that tracks value perfectly but cannot be forecast will be capped by procurement, and a cap is a subscription with extra steps and worse goodwill. The tell in the wild: the customer's first question in a renewal is not "how much?" but "what's the maximum this can be?" The obvious reading — that they are negotiating — is wrong; they are telling you your metric has failed their planning process.

Two: price structure and price level are different decisions, and juniors conflate them. In a two-sided or multi-product business, moving a charge from one side to the other can change total volume dramatically while leaving the total charge identical. The tell: a pricing debate that only ever produces proposals of the form "8.2 percent versus 9 percent". Nobody in the room has proposed changing who is billed, which means nobody is arguing about structure.

Three: a flat price is an underwriting decision. When a firm charges a fixed fee for variable consumption, it has written an insurance policy on its customers' behaviour, and it should be priced and reserved like one — with attention to the tail, not the mean. The tell: blended gross margin drifting down by a point a quarter while every individual cohort looks healthy. The obvious reading is "our costs are rising"; the correct reading is usually "our mix is shifting towards the tail we underwrote".

Four: usage-based revenue has no cancellation event, so churn becomes invisible. A subscription customer who leaves sends a signal on a date. A consumption customer who stops caring simply consumes less, and the revenue decays across months without ever appearing in a churn report. Standard retention instrumentation — logo retention, cancellation reasons — measures nothing useful here. The tell: logo retention flat at 97 percent while revenue per account falls quarter over quarter. Net revenue retention is the only honest number, and the competent practitioner often does not have it broken out by cohort.

Five: a commission is not a revenue model unless the firm cannot be removed from the transaction. This is the single most expensive lesson in marketplace product management. Commissions are durable in categories where the platform holds something the parties cannot replicate — escrow, trust, dispute resolution, logistics, a payment rail, a regulated licence — and decay towards zero where the platform holds only the introduction. The tell: a repeat-purchase rate that looks excellent on first repeat and falls off a cliff at third or fourth. The obvious reading is that the category has low frequency. The correct reading is that the third transaction happened, just not on the platform.

Six: the revenue model decides the gross margin, and later cost discipline cannot undo it. An expert regards mechanism choice as the moment the margin structure is set — thereafter, operational efficiency moves margin by a few points, while mechanism choice moved it by tens. The tell: a company running an efficiency programme to rescue a margin problem created by how it charges. Squeezing cloud spend by twelve percent does not fix a decile that is minus seventy-seven percent.

Seven: a model migration is a cash event before it is a revenue event, and the trough is deeper than the plan. Moving from a one-time charge to a recurring one replaces a lump of cash today with a stream that arrives over years, while the cost base continues to arrive monthly. Adobe's well-documented 2013 move to Creative Cloud produced a visible revenue dip before it produced a much larger recurring business; firms without Adobe's balance sheet do not survive the dip. The tell: a plan whose only chart is annual recurring revenue. If nobody has drawn an eighteen-month cash bridge with a marked low point, the migration has not been planned, only described.

Eight: the customer who pays and the customer the team serves diverge quietly, and the product drifts towards the payer. In advertising models this is stated openly. It is subtler in enterprise software, where the buyer is a procurement committee and the user is an underwriter, and roadmap priorities gradually accumulate around audit logs, single sign-on and compliance reporting — features no user ever asked for and every buyer scores. The tell: a roadmap whose last three quarters would be invisible to a daily user. Not necessarily wrong; but it should be a decision, not a drift.

Nine: the revenue model has to survive the compensation plan. Whatever the mechanism, somebody's variable pay is attached to a number derived from it, and behaviour follows the pay, not the strategy deck. Cutting device price to seed a subscription cuts the hardware salesperson's commission; moving from commission to consumption changes what the marketplace category manager is measured on; introducing overage billing hands the account manager an annual argument with their own customer. The tell: a revenue-model proposal with no accompanying change to the comp plan. The obvious reading is that comp is someone else's problem. The correct reading is that the model will be sold half-heartedly and then declared not to have worked.

7. How this differs by product type and by company stage

In consumer products, user, decider and payer are usually the same person, which makes the revenue model legible but caps it hard at household willingness to pay. In India, where median digital-service ARPU is a small fraction of the United States figure, this constraint bites earlier than it does elsewhere, and it is the main reason so many Indian consumer products are advertising-funded, transaction-funded or cross-subsidised by a financial-services line. That is not a failure of imagination; it is an arithmetic consequence of the price ceiling.

In B2B and enterprise, the three roles split: user, economic buyer, and the signatory who controls the budget line. This splitting, not size, is what pushes enterprise towards annual contracts, seat or capacity pricing and negotiated terms — the model must be explicable to three audiences with different interests, and a mechanism the procurement committee cannot forecast will lose to one it can, even at a higher total price. Dhanika lives here, and it explains why Kulkarni could not simply move to pure metered pricing however well the metric fit.

In platforms and marketplaces, the firm is not a party to the transaction it profits from, so the whole question becomes which side to charge, how heavily, and what the platform holds that prevents the parties from routing around it. Take rate is a political variable as much as an economic one: it is set at a level the participants will tolerate, and tolerance falls as the supply side consolidates. A market with ten thousand atomised carriers tolerates eight percent; the same market after the top two hundred fleets have grown to a third of volume does not.

In hardware and physical goods, margin is bounded below by the bill of materials and above by the shelf price a channel will accept, which leaves far less design freedom than software people expect. The interesting revenue-model work is therefore all in what attaches to the device — consumables, service, software — and in whether the firm can enforce the attachment.

For AI products, the difference is genuine rather than fashionable, for the two reasons given earlier: cost of goods sold is variable and material, and the unit that used to carry the price — the seat — is being eroded by the product's own capability. It is worth saying plainly where the difference is not real: AI products face the same procurement calendars, the same buyer-user split and the same regulatory perimeter as any other enterprise software, and the temptation to treat them as a category exempt from those constraints has produced a good deal of expensive pricing.

Company stage cuts across all of this. At seed and Series A, a single legible mechanism is worth more than an optimal one, because the firm needs one diagnostic number — attach rate, take rate, conversion — that explains the whole business to a small team and a sceptical investor. From Series B onwards, the firm can support a second stream if and only if it has the billing infrastructure and the sales narrative to carry it; the common failure is adding the second stream twelve months before the billing system can invoice it. At scale, multi-stream structures become not just possible but necessary, since each stream has a different growth ceiling. The important stage-specific truth is that the cost of changing a revenue model rises roughly with the number of contracts in force, which means the window for a clean change closes quietly and early.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Dhanika Labs: repairing a flat price without losing the account base

Kulkarni's redesign kept the subscription and rebuilt it as a three-part tariff: a platform fee of ₹1,50,000 per account per year, a seat charge reduced from ₹1,250 to ₹900 per month, an included allowance of 150 document sets per seat per month, and an overage rate of ₹7.50 per set beyond it. The allowance was deliberately set at roughly the eightieth percentile of observed consumption, so that eight deciles of seats would see a lower bill, not a higher one.

What it does is remove the negative tail and compress the distribution: the worst decile moves from minus 77 percent to plus 40 percent, and no decile is loss-making. Total revenue rises from ₹9.60 crore to about ₹12.9 crore and blended gross margin from 61 percent to roughly 72 percent — but the durable result is that Dhanika's margin no longer depends on how successful its customers are.

Two details of execution mattered more than the arithmetic. First, Kulkarni grandfathered the existing terms for two renewal cycles for any account that signed a multi-year extension, which converted a price increase into a commercial negotiation with something to trade. Second, she shipped a consumption dashboard six weeks before the first invoice under the new terms, so that no customer's first experience of the meter was a surprise on a bill. Both are standard practice among people who have done this before and absent from almost every first attempt.

8.2 Dravid Freight Exchange: replacing a leaking commission with two streams that do not leak

Sethi did the opposite of what his board asked. Instead of raising the take rate from 8.2 to 9 percent, he cut it to 4.5 percent and built two new revenue lines beside it. The first was a subscription sold to fleet owners — ₹1,800 per truck per month for a dispatch, telematics, e-way-bill and driver-payout workbench that a fleet came to run its operations on, whether or not the load originated on Dravid. The second was an arrangement fee of 0.9 percent on freight-bill discounting and fuel credit, originated by Dravid and underwritten by a partner NBFC, with Dravid's first-loss exposure held inside the five percent ceiling set by the RBI's digital lending rules.

That is a claim on the customer that survives the transaction, which is what a commission never was.

8.3 Dhanush Devices: a revenue-model change that nearly destroyed a profitable company

Dhanush Devices, of Coimbatore, made smart water meters and sold them outright to urban local bodies and large housing societies: ₹6,200 per meter against ₹4,350 of bill of materials and installation, a gross margin of ₹1,850 or thirty percent. In the year to March 2025 it shipped 62,000 units, booked ₹38.4 crore of revenue and ₹11.5 crore of gross profit, and was modestly profitable.

Its board, advised that recurring revenue commanded a materially higher valuation multiple, approved a shift to "metering as a service": Dhanush would retain ownership of the meter and charge ₹110 per connection per month on a seven-year contract. The arithmetic looked defensible. Monthly operating cost per connection — connectivity, cloud, field maintenance — was ₹26, leaving ₹84 of contribution. Against ₹4,350 of capital per connection, simple payback was 51.8 months.

The discounted arithmetic was less kind, and nobody ran it before the decision. At a 15 percent cost of capital, or 1.25 percent a month, the present value of ₹84 a month for 84 months is ₹84 × 51.82 = ₹4,353 — against ₹4,350 of capital deployed. The contract was, to within three rupees, exactly net-present-value neutral before any allowance for meter failure, contract cancellation, or the collection behaviour of municipal customers. Every rupee of margin in the old model had been converted into a seven-year zero-NPV annuity, and the firm had paid for the privilege with its balance sheet.

Figure 3. The same connection, two mechanisms. The outright sale banks ₹1,850 immediately and moves on. Metering as a service is ₹4,350 in the hole on day one and does not return to zero until month 52 — and that is before municipal receivables at 240 days, which push the real crossing towards month 60. Multiplied by the 48,000 connections Dhanush deployed in fourteen months, the day-one hole was ₹20.9 crore.

What actually happened was worse than the chart. Dhanush deployed 48,000 connections in fourteen months, funding ₹20.9 crore of meter capital with debt at 13.8 percent. Reported revenue from those connections at full deployment was ₹110 × 48,000 × 12, or ₹6.3 crore a year, against the ₹38.4 crore the company had booked the year before from outright sales. Revenue fell by more than eighty percent in the transition year while cash went out at speed. Municipal payment cycles ran at 240 days. By the third quarter of the transition, Dhanush had breached the net-debt-to-EBITDA covenant on its working capital facility.

The recovery, which took nineteen months, had three parts and none of them was heroic. First, the contract was restructured into a hybrid: a ₹3,200 upfront capital contribution per connection — payable from state and central urban infrastructure grants the municipal customer already held — plus ₹62 per month for seven years. This recovered 74 percent of the capital on installation and left a genuinely recurring, genuinely profitable annuity on top. Second, the monthly receivable stream was assigned to an NBFC at a discount, converting a seven-year annuity into near-term cash and moving collection risk to a party better equipped to price it. Third, and most tellingly, Dhanush reverted to outright sales for housing societies, which pay in thirty days, and reserved the service model for grant-funded municipal projects where a third party was actually paying the capital. The company raised ₹28 crore in a flat bridge round to survive the gap. The lesson Ravi Subramanian, its chief executive, now states at every conference he is invited to, is not that recurring revenue is bad. It is that a recurring revenue model is a financing decision wearing a product costume, and that it should have been run past the treasurer before the board.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of catching them late

Table 5 — Seven failure modes. The early warning is the metric that moves first; the diagnostic is the question that confirms it in under a week.

The pattern across all seven is worth naming. Every one of them is detectable months earlier in a distribution than in an average, and almost every company monitors averages. Blended gross margin, overall retention, total GMV, aggregate revenue — each of these is an average that stays comfortable while its tail rots. The single highest-leverage habit in this domain is to keep every revenue metric ranked rather than summed, and to read the bottom decile monthly.

10. Where competent people genuinely disagree

Seats or consumption for AI products. The consumption camp argues that when a product's marginal cost is real and its capability erodes headcount, per-seat pricing guarantees that vendor revenue falls as customer value rises; their evidence is the expansion behaviour of metered infrastructure businesses and the first cohorts of agentic products whose seat counts declined at renewal. The seat camp argues that enterprise budgets are annual and committee-approved, that a variable bill converts every renewal into a fresh procurement fight, and that the observed outcome of aggressive metering is a spend cap and a home-grown substitute for the expensive workloads. What would have to be true for the consumption camp to be wrong: that buyers' tolerance for variance does not rise even as metered billing becomes the norm across their software estate. What would have to be true for the seat camp to be wrong: that seat counts hold up under agentic products — and the early evidence is that in some workflows they do not.

High take rate or low. One position holds that take rate should be set near the value the platform demonstrably adds, that low take rates are a subsidy funded by investors rather than a strategy, and that platforms which under-charge simply transfer their margin to their suppliers without buying loyalty. The other holds that take rate is a tax on the ecosystem that determines how fast the ecosystem grows and how hard participants work to escape it, and that the durable platforms are those that kept the rate low enough that leaving was never worth the effort. The evidence on both sides is real and comes from different categories: high-take-rate models persist where the platform holds the payment rail, the trust layer or the demand; low-take-rate discipline has preserved categories where the parties could easily transact directly. For the high-rate position to be wrong, leakage would have to be a function of rate rather than of platform-held assets. For the low-rate position to be wrong, the growth bought by a low rate would have to fail to convert into any durable advantage — which, in several Indian categories, is exactly what has happened.

Should recurring revenue be pursued for its own sake? The affirmative case is that recurring revenue lowers the cost of capital, smooths planning, raises valuation multiples and creates a customer relationship rather than a series of transactions. The sceptical case, which Dhanush Devices learned expensively, is that recurring revenue is frequently a financing structure in disguise: the firm converts cash today into an annuity, and unless the return on that annuity exceeds the firm's true cost of capital — including the risk that the customer stops paying — it has destroyed value while improving the shape of its revenue chart. For the affirmative to be wrong, the valuation premium on recurring revenue would have to be smaller than the capital cost of creating it, which is precisely the situation for capital-intensive hardware. For the sceptical case to be wrong, the strategic and retention benefits would have to be large enough to justify a near-zero-NPV annuity, which is sometimes genuinely true when the annuity also blocks a competitor.

Does the revenue model follow the value metric or the budget line? This is the cleanest disagreement of the four and the one most likely to arise in a real meeting. The value-metric position is a claim about fairness and long-run alignment. The budget-line position is a claim about how purchasing decisions are actually made in organisations. They conflict most sharply in enterprise software sold to regulated industries, where the metric that tracks value best is precisely the one no buyer can commit to in advance. The three-part tariff is often described as the resolution, but it is better understood as a truce: it gives each camp its term in the formula without settling which term should dominate when they conflict.

11. What mastery looks like

The person who has merely studied revenue models can name six archetypes and produce a plausible recommendation. The person who has internalised them behaves differently in five observable ways.

They open with the distribution, not the average. Asked about a company's margin, they ask for it ranked by account before they will discuss it. They treat the mechanism as the moment margin is decided, so they resist the framing that a margin problem is an efficiency problem. They ask, early and without embarrassment, who inside the company loses if the proposal succeeds — because they have watched an arithmetically correct recommendation die in a corridor conversation with a sales leader whose commission plan it broke. They insist on a cash bridge alongside every recurring-revenue plan, and they can say, without looking it up, roughly where the low point falls and whether the company survives it. And when they propose a new stream, they name the person who owns its billing and the system that will invoice it, because they know that the practical constraint on multi-stream models is almost never strategy and almost always the invoicing.

There is a sixth habit, harder to see. They can state plainly which customers their revenue model is designed to exclude. A firm that cannot answer that question has not chosen a model; it has drifted into one and is hoping the average holds.

12. What each of them decided

Kulkarni took the three-part tariff to Dhanika's board on 14 April 2026 with three numbers and one concession. The numbers were the decile table, the projected move in blended gross margin from 61 to roughly 72 percent, and the honest downside: if her assumed 18 percent behavioural reduction in heavy usage turned out to be 40 percent, revenue uplift would be closer to twelve percent than thirty-four, though the margin floor would hold either way. The concession was that she would not touch the seven deciles that were working; the allowance was set so that 80 percent of seats saw a lower bill. She also rewrote the account-management compensation plan in the same paper, moving it from booked ARR to gross profit per account, on the argument that she could not ask a team to defend a margin they were not paid for. The board approved it. The first quarter under the new terms lost four accounts, all in the heaviest decile, and all four had been unprofitable.

Sethi did not get his board's approval at the first attempt. The proposal to cut take rate from 8.2 percent to 4.5 percent was read, correctly, as a thirty-three percent cut in revenue, and the board declined it in March. He returned in July with Tan's leakage cohort analysis extended by twelve months, showing that the 27 percent ninety-day leak compounded to 44 percent by month twelve on the platform's best lanes, and with a pilot: 900 trucks in the Gurugram–Nagpur corridor on the ₹1,800 subscription at a 4.5 percent take rate. On those lanes, ninety-day leakage had fallen to 13 percent and contribution per truck had risen. The board approved a staged rollout with the take rate cut phased over four quarters rather than one. Sethi's private view, which he did not share with the board, was that the subscription was not really a revenue model at all — it was a retention mechanism that happened to be billable, and its value lay less in the ₹30 crore it would produce than in the ₹40 crore of commission it would stop losing.

Discussion question one. Dravid's three-stream plan produces slightly less revenue than its commission-only model. Under what circumstances is a board right to reject a plan that lowers revenue while raising contribution, and what would it need to see to be confident this is not simply a slower way of shrinking?

Discussion question two. Dhanush Devices' metering-as-a-service contract was exactly NPV-neutral at a 15 percent cost of capital. Suppose it had been clearly NPV-positive — say ₹95 a month of contribution instead of ₹84. Would the transition still have been a mistake, and if so, what does that tell you about the difference between a good contract and a good business model?

Discussion question three. Kulkarni changed the compensation plan in the same document as the revenue model. Sethi did not. Identify the specific behaviours Dravid's category managers are still being paid for under the new structure, and say what you would change first.

13. Going deeper

  1. What a business model is — the creation half that revenue models only capture from; read it to see why a mechanism cannot rescue a weak value proposition.
  2. Subscription economics — cohort retention, churn and lifetime value done properly; it turns Kulkarni's run-rate into a durability claim.
  3. Advertising business models — the only archetype where the payer and the user are structurally different people, and the consequences for product priorities.
  4. Marketplace economics — liquidity, matching and why take rate is bounded by what participants tolerate, not by what value is added.
  5. Hardware business models — bill-of-materials floors, channel economics and the attach problem that undid Dhanush Devices.
  6. Licensing, OEM and white-label — near-perfect operating leverage bought at the price of losing the end-customer relationship.
  7. Payments, float and financial revenue — where the real margin sits in many Indian platforms, and the regulatory perimeter that governs it.
  8. Open-source and open-core models — distribution bought with free software and monetised at a deliberately drawn boundary.
  9. Direct-to-consumer and retail models for goods — what changes when you own the channel and carry the inventory risk yourself.
  10. When to charge — the timing question the archetypes leave implicit: at signup, at value delivery, or after outcome.
  11. The value metric — the single most consequential sub-decision inside any recurring model; read it directly after this page.
  12. Game and gamified product economies — virtual goods and in-app purchase, where willingness to pay is manufactured rather than discovered.
  13. Professional services and packaged services — the margin-diluting stream every enterprise product eventually acquires, and how to contain it.
  14. Hybrid and multi-stream business models — the composition problem Dravid is now living, including who owns billing for each stream.
  15. Business Model and Lean Canvas — the one-page tools that put revenue streams next to cost structure where they belong.
  16. Freemium as a business model — conversion arithmetic and the cost of serving users who will never pay.
  17. Usage-based and consumption models — the mechanics of metering, allowances and overage, in far more depth than section three allowed.
  18. Cost structure and operating leverage — the other half of the margin equation, and the reason a fixed-cost base changes which mechanism is viable.
  19. Changing a business model — the migration playbook: grandfathering, phasing, cash bridges and the compensation plan.
  20. Marketplace unit economics in depth — contribution per transaction, cohort payback and the leakage instrumentation Tan had to build from scratch.

Dhanika Labs, Dravid Freight Exchange and Dhanush Devices are fictional companies constructed for teaching purposes; their numbers are illustrative and internally consistent but not drawn from any real firm's accounts. Regulators, statutes and market conditions referred to — the Reserve Bank of India's payment-aggregator and digital-lending frameworks, IRDAI commission caps, the zero-MDR regime on UPI, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, and Ind AS 115 — are real and are described as context only.

Mandai Commerce Systems: What Should We Charge For?

A Pune distribution-software company, a clause from 2023 that governs how it can charge, and a board meeting in the morning.

1. The night before

At twenty past nine on the evening of Sunday 29 November 2026, the third floor of Mandai Commerce Systems' office off Baner Road in Pune held four people. Yastika Ghadge, who had founded the company seven years earlier, had the board pack open and a page beside it with four headings and nothing under any of them.

The board met at ten. The item was listed as Revenue architecture: FY2028 and beyond, Yamaji Gangal's phrasing, not hers. What it would actually ask was simpler. Mandai had spent seven years being paid a monthly fee for software, and in the last fourteen months had started being paid in two further ways, neither of them large. Someone had to say which was the business.

Mahaganga Distribution's notice on its eleven contracts fell due on 31 December. Cash at bank on 1 November had been ₹612 lakh. Yastika could construct a defensible case under each of the four headings, which she understood to be the problem rather than the solution.

2. How Mandai got here

Mandai was founded in March 2019 by Yastika Ghadge and two colleagues from a Pune pharmaceutical distributor. The first price was ₹9,000 a month, set by asking three customers what they paid their accountant.

By August 2021 the company had signed its first multi-state distributor and found it consumed eleven times the support of a district account. The tiering held until November 2022, when single-town churn ran at nineteen accounts in a quarter and Mandai introduced a ₹7,500 band to stop it. The band was meant to last two renewals.

In February 2023 Mandai raised ₹28 crore, rather less than half from a financial investor and the rest from Mahaganga Distribution Pvt Ltd, a national FMCG group already Mandai's largest customer, whose eleven operating companies sat in the top tier. The agreement did three things: it fixed those eleven contracts at ₹1,10,000 a month to 31 March 2029, with a minimum of ₹1.45 crore a year; it barred Mandai from charging any other distributor less per outlet served than Mahaganga paid; and it barred conversion of those contracts to a usage or fee basis without written consent. Nobody wrote down what the clause would mean if the price stopped being a monthly fee.

3. The industry

India's packaged-goods and pharmaceutical trade reaches its customers through roughly thirteen million small outlets served by distributors who buy, warehouse and break bulk. Software reached that layer from three directions, each charging differently.

Udaan and Jumbotail built their positions on order value. Reliance Retail gave its ordering software away through Metro Cash & Carry and JioMart Partner, because it earned on the goods. ONDC made the protocol layer a public good. Zoho and Freshworks had taught the market that software costs a per-seat monthly fee, so a salesperson quoting ₹18,500 a month was compared, silently, with a Zoho licence.

Three rules bore on the choice. Under the RBI's payment-aggregator framework Mandai could not hold customer funds: settlement ran through Razorpay, so a fee on money moving was a fee on somebody else's rail. The DPDP Act, 2023 governed whether order history could sell a placement. GST e-invoicing, mandatory above ₹5 crore of turnover, gave Mandai a second, independent measure of what its customers sold — which is how the trouble in Exhibit 5 was found.

The exposure was not only Indian. A three-year contract with Mawrid Foodstuff Trading LLC in Dubai, signed in AED and recorded within subscription revenue, licensed the platform to run under Mawrid's own name. A desk in Edison, New Jersey sold to South Asian grocery distributors in the north-east United States, where the installed base was small and the contracts were not.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

The belief in February 2023 was that subscription would compound with the number of distributors, that number with the sales team, and price per distributor with the tiering. For two years it did: Exhibit 1 shows it rising from ₹742 lakh in FY2024 to ₹1,268 lakh in FY2026.

Three things then happened. In September 2025 a first pilot charged a small group a percentage of order value settled through the Razorpay rail instead of a monthly fee, producing ₹97 lakh in the seven months to 31 March 2026. In January 2026 four FMCG brands paid for placement on the ordering screens, producing ₹41 lakh in three months. In April 2026 a second, larger pilot — thirty distributors, twenty Tier C and ten Tier D, subscription waived — began the run in Exhibit 3.

Two beliefs have since failed. The first was that subscription per distributor was a proxy for value delivered: Exhibit 2 gives each tier's equivalent fee rate on routed order value, and the four do not line up — the single-town band of November 2022 sits above the multi-state band. The second was that the order log was the only number the business needed. In October 2026 finance reconciled twelve months of routed order value against the GST e-invoice data customers file; the two differ by ₹629 crore, 12.1 per cent of the log figure, and nobody has established which a fee should ride on.

The platform recorded 21,400 retail outlets placing orders in the month to 30 September 2026. That count has never been split across the tiers against the distributors' own records.

5. The people

Yastika Ghadge, founder and chief executive, Pune. Wants a model she can still change in three years; her 19 per cent and her secondary turn on the FY2028 multiple. She has not told the board the 2023 clause was her mistake.

Yamaji Gangal, chief financial officer, Pune. Wants predictability; his bonus is written on FY2028 revenue growth and cash. He has run the pilot's September month out to a year and shown Yastika the result. He has not circulated the ₹629 crore gap beyond three people.

Yug Ghanwat, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru. Wants one decision, not four pilots. Option 2's rail work would cost two quarters of a roadmap committed to the placement console. He is privately certain the order log is the wrong base and has never said so in writing.

Yesaji Gunjal, head of international sales, Edison, New Jersey. Wants annual contracted value, which is what his quota is in. He has not said Mawrid's renewal has moved to a licence fee with a volume cap he agreed verbally.

Yvonne Gerstner, principal designer, Berlin. Wants the ordering screen uncluttered, and argues placement and a fee are two bills for one event. Her consulting agreement renews in April. She has not said she would resign over a rate card.

Yannick Grondin, head of data science, Toronto. Wants the fee model, because its data is the asset he was hired to build. He holds that placement sells a brand a demand forecast, not screen space. He has not disclosed that his October elasticity estimate rests on eleven distributors, not thirty.

Yoganjali Gavas, customer-success lead, Singapore. Wants the Tier D band kept; reports the pilot distributors took the waiver not because they preferred a fee but because the subscription was the only visible line in their accounts. Her target is account count, which the waiver flatters. She has not said four of the thirty want out.

Yudhishthir Godambe, nominee director for Mahaganga Distribution, Mumbai. Wants the clause honoured and the renewal signed. His group's margin improves if Mandai's software is cheap and ubiquitous. He has not said Mahaganga's board has asked what Mandai would cost to buy.

8. The options as Yastika sees them

The board pack set the four headings out as a choice of one. Yvonne's comment on the draft asked why it was a choice of one; Yannick's call, why there were four.

Option 1: hold the subscription and re-tier. Tier C moves to ₹24,000 a month and the Tier D band is retired at renewal — 161 of the 265 Tier C and D contracts renew on 1 April 2027 and the other 104 on 1 October 2027. Retraining and papering cost ₹18 lakh; engineering is nil. The pilot thirty are inside those counts and stay on the waiver. Any new band is subject to the per-outlet test.

Option 2: convert Tiers C and D to a fee. A fee of 0.85 per cent on order value settled through the rail replaces the subscription for those tiers at renewal, on the same two dates. Rail and reconciliation engineering costs ₹64 lakh across two quarters of Yug's roadmap. The payment partner's discount on settled value is charged at 0.19 per cent. Tiers A and B are not converted, and the eleven Mahaganga contracts, which the agreement bars from conversion without consent, are untouched.

Option 3: licence the platform. A term sheet dated 19 November 2026 from a private-sector bank's merchant-services arm offers ₹6.2 crore over three years — ₹1.8 crore in year one, ₹2.1 crore in year two, ₹2.3 crore in year three — for a white-labelled build serving the bank's current-account distributors, Mandai's name removed. Delivery requires nine ring-fenced engineers costing ₹2.4 crore a year fully loaded, against the headcount freeze. The counterparty is not among the four groups named in the 2023 exclusivity.

Option 4: sell the attention and widen the base. The ordering screens open to brand-funded placement on a published rate card, and the hardware resale margin is cut to put devices into more outlets. An advertising desk of four costs ₹52 lakh a year; the consent rebuild the DPDP Act requires before order history can be used for targeting is quoted at ₹31 lakh. Subscription is untouched. Hardware revenue falls by whatever the margin cut gives away.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Money. The ₹450 lakh term facility drawn in June 2024 requires at least ₹350 lakh of cash at each quarter end, tested on 31 December 2026 and 31 March 2027; Exhibit 6 is the forecast on the current model.

People. Headcount is frozen at 118 until 31 March 2027; Yug's team is 34 of those.

Regulation. Brand targeting on order history requires the DPDP Act consent architecture, which does not exist today.

Contracts. Mahaganga must notify by Thursday 31 December 2026 how many of its eleven operating companies stay on the platform from 1 April 2027; the February 2023 terms run to 31 March 2029 and the exclusivity over four named groups to April 2028. The bank's term sheet expires on 15 January 2027; Mawrid's licence renews on 1 April 2027. The papering timetable treats 24 November and 25 December 2026 as working days in Pune; the holiday list places Guru Nanak Jayanti on 24 November and Mumbai has not confirmed it, so if that day is not worked the notice loses a day.

10. Questions for discussion

  2. Exhibit 2 measures routed order value from the order log; Exhibit 5 measures the same twelve months from the e-invoice reconciliation. Decide which a fee should be levied on, and what you would need before defending that choice to a Tier C distributor.
  3. Exhibit 3 gives six months of the Phase-2 pilot. Estimate the cohort's fee revenue for the twelve months to 30 September 2027 on assumptions you state, and say which of them the exhibit lets you test.

  6. It is Monday morning, 30 November 2026, and Yastika has ninety minutes with her board. What should she do about the revenue model, what should she tell it she does not know, and what should she put in front of Yudhishthir Godambe before 31 December?

11. Sunday, 11:40 p.m.

The others had gone by eleven. Yastika stayed for something not in the pack: a printout of the cohort's September invoices, thirty lines, sent by Yoganjali at half past one on Sunday morning Singapore time — eleven on Saturday night in Pune. Four of the thirty carried a remark typed into the same field by four account managers, in four phrasings, all asking the same thing.

She put the sheet face down and opened the pack at the page headed Recommendation, still blank. Outside, the traffic on Baner Road had thinned to the long-distance trucks going north, each carrying somebody's stock to somebody's shop. She had until ten.

Strategy & Business — Business Models

Revenue Models

Which way of charging fits this product, and what does each trade off?

1. A ring that made money once

On the second Tuesday of August 2026, Meera Iyer, chief product officer at Ratnika Circle, carried two spreadsheets into a board meeting at the company’s Indiranagar office in Bengaluru, along with one question she still could not answer with full confidence: was Ratnika Circle a hardware company that happened to have an app, or a software company that happened to ship a ring?

The distinction was not academic. Ratnika Circle made a smart fitness ring — the Circle Band — that tracked sleep, heart-rate variability and recovery, sold through its own website and through Croma and Reliance Digital outlets, priced at ₹4,999. The ring cost ₹3,600 to build, certify and land in a warehouse, which meant every unit sold put ₹1,399 of gross profit on the books, a margin of just under 28 percent. In the financial year that had just closed, Ratnika Circle had sold 40,000 rings and booked ₹5.60 crore of gross profit doing it. That was the entire business model: make a ring, sell a ring, repeat.

The board, and in particular the firm’s lead investor from Peak XV Partners, wanted something else before it would commit to a Series C round the company hoped to close by the first quarter of 2027: a revenue line that did not reset to zero every January. “You have forty thousand happy customers,” the partner had told Meera on a call the week before, “and as far as I can tell, you make money from each of them exactly once.” Competitors — most visibly the American company Whoop, and a well-funded Bengaluru rival closer to home — had already layered a paid coaching subscription on top of their hardware, and were being valued as recurring-revenue businesses rather than device makers. Ratnika Circle’s own product team had built something similar: a coaching and analytics layer, priced at ₹499 a month, sitting mostly unused in the app because nobody had decided how aggressively to sell it, or what to do to the price of the ring if they did.

Meera’s task for the board meeting was to recommend a revenue model — not a price, a model — and to show the arithmetic behind it. Get it right, and Ratnika Circle would walk into its Series C as a subscription business with a hardware moat. Get it wrong, and it would either strand a coaching product nobody paid for, or cut hardware margin to the bone and discover, eighteen months later, that the recurring revenue never showed up to replace what it gave up.

2. The idea

A revenue model is the specific mechanism by which a company converts the value it creates into cash it actually collects: who pays, for what unit of value, how often, and whether the price moves with how much value the customer receives. It is one output of a larger design process — the full business model, which also covers the value proposition, the channels used to reach customers, and the cost structure needed to deliver — but the revenue model answers only the capture half of that equation: given that value has been created, how does money move from the customer’s account into the company’s?

The vocabulary practitioners now use to sort revenue models settled into something like its current form through two overlapping efforts, built less on a single inventor’s flash of insight than on the slower academic habit of arranging recurring patterns. In 2001, MIT Sloan researchers Peter Weill and Michael Vitale catalogued a set of recurring “atomic business models” they observed across early e-business ventures, and the revenue mechanism was one of the dimensions they used to tell one model from another. A few years later, Alexander Osterwalder’s Business Model Canvas — developed around 2008 and popularised in the book Business Model Generation in 2010 — gave “Revenue Streams” a formal box on the page, sitting beside “Cost Structure” as the two building blocks that decide whether a company built to deliver value can also survive delivering it. It is this second framing — revenue model as one of nine deliberate design choices, not something that falls out automatically once the product is built — that most business programmes now teach, usually paired with a teardown exercise: take an existing company and work backward from its income statement to the revenue mechanism actually generating each line.

The single sentence Meera could repeat in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: a revenue model is not a price, it is the choice of what a customer is charged for, who that customer actually is, and how often the charge repeats — and every one of those choices quietly decides who the company is really building the product for.

3. How it actually works

In practice, choosing a revenue model means working through six archetypes that between them cover almost every product a reader will encounter, and then running a short sequence of questions that experienced practitioners perform instinctively rather than explicitly — which is precisely why it is worth making them explicit.

The six archetypes, described plainly: a subscription charges a recurring fee for ongoing access to a product or service, regardless of how much the customer actually uses it in a given period. A transaction or usage fee charges per discrete event — per ride, per message sent, per API call — so revenue scales directly with activity. A commission, most often seen in marketplaces, takes a percentage of a transaction that happens between two other parties the platform merely connects; the platform is neither the buyer nor the seller, only the intermediary paid for making the match happen. Advertising charges a third party — a brand, an agency — for access to the attention or data of a user who is not the one paying, which means the free user is the product being sold, not the customer being served. Licensing charges a fee, often a royalty per unit or a flat annual sum, for the right to use a company’s intellectual property, brand or technology, typically without the licensor ever touching the end customer — Rachna Vision, a Bengaluru firm that built a fall-detection computer-vision algorithm, illustrates this cleanly: it licenses the algorithm to wearable-hardware manufacturers for a royalty of roughly ₹40 per device shipped, and never sells a single unit to a consumer itself. And hardware margin, the model Ratnika Circle had relied on exclusively, charges once for a physical good, capturing value as the spread between what the unit costs to build and land and what the customer pays for it.

Table 1 — Six revenue-model archetypes, and who actually pays
