Having named the six, the harder and more implicit step is deciding which one — or which combination — fits a specific product, and that decision runs through a short sequence most experienced product leaders perform without ever narrating it aloud. First, identify the actual unit of value being delivered: is it ongoing access, a completed job, a successful match, an audience, a right to use, or a durable good? Second, identify who captures that value and whether that person is the same person who will be asked to pay — a fitness ring’s user and payer are the same person, but a free news app’s reader and payer usually are not. Third, decide how often the charge should repeat: once, per event, or continuously, which is really a decision about whether the company wants a relationship or a sale. Fourth, decide whether the price should scale with the value the customer realises — known as choosing a value metric — or stay flat regardless of use. Fifth, and the step most often skipped, model the gross margin the chosen mechanism will actually produce once servicing costs are subtracted, because a subscription with high support costs can carry a worse margin than the hardware sale it was meant to replace. And sixth, check the cash-flow timing the model implies: a hardware sale is collected and recognised immediately, while a subscription is collected in instalments and often recognised as deferred revenue over the period it covers, which changes how much cash is actually in the bank at any one moment even when the accounting revenue lines look identical.

Figure 1. Steps one through five of the sequence; step six, checking cash-flow timing against deferred revenue, is discussed in the worked example that follows.

4. A worked example

Put the sequence to work on Ratnika Circle’s own numbers, because a diagram is only useful once it survives contact with a real income statement.

Start with what already existed. The Circle Band sold at ₹4,999 against a landed cost of ₹3,600, a gross margin of ₹1,399 per unit, or just under 28 percent. At 40,000 units in the year just closed, that produced ₹5.60 crore of gross profit (40,000 × ₹1,399 = ₹5,59,60,000) — all of it earned once per customer, at the moment of sale, with nothing more to collect from that customer unless they bought a second ring.

The proposal on the table was to cut the hardware margin almost to the bone — drop the price to ₹3,999, just ₹399 over cost, a margin of 10 percent — and use the lower price to remove friction from adoption, while selling the ₹499-a-month coaching subscription hard as the business’s real profit engine. Assume the coaching product, once built, costs relatively little to serve at scale — cloud compute, a lean coaching-content team, support — leaving roughly 80 percent of subscription revenue as gross profit, or ₹399.20 per subscriber per month.

At the same 40,000 units sold, hardware gross profit falls to ₹1.60 crore (40,000 × ₹399 = ₹1,59,60,000). To be worth the trade, the subscription has to make up the ₹4.00 crore shortfall, and then some. Everything now turns on a number product teams often treat as a footnote: attach rate, the share of ring buyers who actually keep paying for the subscription.

Ratnika’s product team’s working assumption, based on a six-week pilot with 1,200 existing owners, was a 45 percent attach rate. At that rate, 18,000 of the 40,000 buyers become paying subscribers, generating ₹71.86 lakh of subscription gross profit a month (18,000 × ₹399.20), an annualised run-rate of ₹8.62 crore. Added to the ₹1.60 crore still coming from hardware, the hybrid model’s steady-state annual gross profit is ₹10.22 crore — nearly double the ₹5.60 crore the pure-hardware model produced. And unlike the hardware number, next year’s cohort of 40,000 buyers adds to that run-rate rather than replacing it, because most subscribers from this year are still paying next year too.

Run the same arithmetic with the input the board was actually nervous about — attach rate — set to a far more conservative 20 percent, closer to what a skeptical partner might assume if the coaching content proved less sticky than the pilot suggested. Only 8,000 buyers subscribe, producing ₹31.94 lakh of subscription gross profit a month, or ₹3.83 crore annualised. Added to the ₹1.60 crore of thinner hardware margin, the hybrid model now yields ₹5.43 crore — slightly less than the ₹5.60 crore the old, pure-hardware model produced on the same 40,000 units. Somewhere between 20 percent and 45 percent sits the model’s breakeven point, and it can be found directly: the ₹4.00 crore of hardware margin given up must be recovered from subscription profit, and each percentage point of attach rate is worth roughly ₹19.16 lakh of annual profit at full scale (40,000 × ₹399.20 × 12 = ₹19.16 crore at 100 percent attach), so the breakeven attach rate is ₹4.00 crore ÷ ₹19.16 crore, or approximately 21 percent. Below 21 percent attach, cutting the hardware margin destroys value; above it, the hybrid model creates value, and the gap widens every month that subscribers who joined this year keep paying next year.

Figure 2. The hybrid model beats the old hardware-only model once attach rate clears roughly 21 percent; at the pilot’s 45 percent, it very nearly doubles annual gross profit.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Revenue model is not pricing model

A revenue model decides the mechanism — subscription versus transaction versus commission — while a pricing model decides the number attached to that mechanism, using cost-plus, competitor benchmarking or value-based logic. Teams that muddle the two often believe they have “changed the business model” when they have only moved a price up or down within the same mechanism, which explains nothing about why a subscription retains customers differently from a one-time sale, regardless of what either costs.

The payer and the beneficiary are not always the same person

Advertising models make this starkest: the reader of a free news app receives the value, but the advertiser pays for it, which means the product’s real customer — the one whose preferences the team must actually optimise for — is the advertiser, not the reader. A team that forgets this will keep improving the experience for the person who never signs the cheque.

Revenue and take-rate are not the same line, in a marketplace

Raagini Health’s nursing marketplace processes far more money than it earns: a ₹2,000 home-nursing booking produces only the platform’s 18 percent commission, ₹360, as actual revenue, with the remaining ₹1,640 passing through to the nurse. Confusing gross transaction value with revenue inflates a company’s apparent size and can mislead a board into approving a cost structure the real revenue line cannot support.

Choosing a revenue model does not fix a weak value proposition or a broken cost structure

The mechanism only decides how existing value gets captured; it says nothing about whether customers will pay for that value at all, or whether the company can deliver it profitably. A subscription layered onto a product nobody wanted simply converts a one-time disappointment into a recurring one.

Regulation narrows the menu before the team ever gets to choose

In India, a company handling recurring payments, stored value or lending has to work within the Reserve Bank of India’s rules on payment aggregators, prepaid instruments and digital lending, and these rules can rule out an otherwise attractive commission or subscription structure outright, or require a licensed partner to run it — a constraint Ratnika Circle did not face selling a ring, but would face instantly if its coaching subscription ever bundled insurance or financing.

Lock-in behaves differently across the six archetypes

A subscription earns retention through habit and switching cost; a hardware sale earns none of that unless it is deliberately paired with a recurring consumable or service, the “razor and blades” pattern that Ratnika Circle’s hybrid model was really attempting, in a modern form. A commission model’s lock-in lives in the network of buyers and sellers already on the platform, not in the product itself.

What none of this tells you

Knowing which archetype fits a product says nothing about willingness to pay, nothing about whether 45 percent of customers or 4 percent will actually subscribe, and nothing about whether a competitor will undercut the price before the model has time to compound. Those numbers come from pilots, cohort data and competitive intelligence, never from the model’s category alone. It is also worth noting what the run-rate arithmetic above deliberately leaves out: it assumes subscribers stay flat at steady state, and says nothing about how long any single subscriber actually keeps paying. If monthly churn runs at roughly 3 percent, implying about 70 percent of subscribers are still paying at month twelve, the average subscriber lifetime works out to only around thirty-three months — a number the run-rate figure never surfaces on its own, and one Meera would still need before she could tell the board the subscription line was durable rather than merely large today.

The question a thoughtful newcomer should ask before relying on any of it

Who inside my own company benefits, and who is hurt, by the shift I am proposing? A sales team paid commission on hardware revenue will resist a move that cuts device price to ₹3,999, even if the company’s total profit rises, because their own number falls. A finance team optimising for this quarter’s revenue will resist a shift to deferred subscription revenue, even if it is the healthier long-run choice, because near-term reported revenue looks smaller. The revenue model that is correct for the company is not automatically the one that is comfortable for the people inside it, and ignoring that gap is how a mathematically sound recommendation quietly dies in a hallway conversation the deck never anticipated.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early versus large

In a consumer product like the Circle Band, the person who uses the product, decides to buy it, and pays for it are almost always the same individual, which keeps the revenue model relatively legible: price low enough for an impulse or considered personal purchase, and if a subscription is layered on, price it in the range a household budgets without a procurement process — hence ₹499 a month rather than ₹4,990. In B2B software, those three roles routinely split apart: the person using a Raagini Health scheduling tool every day is a nurse coordinator, the person deciding to buy it is a hospital’s operations head, and the person who signs the cheque is procurement or finance, often working from an annual budget cycle rather than a monthly impulse. That split is why B2B revenue models lean toward annual contracts, per-seat or per-facility pricing, and negotiated terms rather than the self-serve monthly subscription that works for consumers — the sales motion has to persuade three different people, not one, and a contract that resets every year gives the vendor a natural point to renegotiate as the hospital’s usage grows.

Marketplace and platform products add a third structural wrinkle: the company is not a party to the transaction it profits from, which means its revenue model has to be built entirely around facilitating, and taking a cut of, value it does not itself produce. Raagini Health, connecting home-nurses with patients across Pune and Nagpur, could not simply charge a subscription to patients without first building enough supply of nurses to make the subscription worth anything — the classic chicken-and-egg problem of two-sided markets — so its earliest revenue-model choice was less about which archetype to pick and more about which side to charge first, and how lightly, to avoid starving the other side of the match.

Company stage changes the calculus again, independent of consumer, B2B or marketplace category. An early-stage company is usually better served running one clean, simple revenue model, because a simple model is easier to explain to investors, easier for a small sales team to sell without help, and easier to diagnose when it underperforms — a single number, attach rate or take rate or conversion, tells the whole story. A large, mature company can run several revenue models simultaneously, layered on top of each other, because it has the billing infrastructure, the sales organisation and the customer trust to sustain the complexity: Amazon captures a retail margin on goods it sells directly, a commission from third-party sellers on its marketplace, a subscription fee through Prime, an advertising fee from brands bidding for placement, and a cloud-computing fee through AWS, all inside one company, without confusing any individual customer about what they are being asked to pay for in that specific interaction. Ratnika Circle, with 40,000 customers and one product line, was not yet that company, which is part of why Meera’s recommendation had to be a single hybrid model — hardware plus one subscription — rather than the sprawling five-stream structure a company ten times its size might run.

7. Common mistakes

Copying a competitor’s revenue model without checking whether the underlying value metric transfers. The symptom is pricing that customers describe as arbitrary or unrelated to what they actually value, visible in support tickets and churn-survey comments rather than in the price itself. The underlying misunderstanding is that a mechanism works for one company because it is anchored to a value metric — API calls, seats, gross transaction value — that fits how that specific product delivers value; borrowing the mechanism without the underlying fit borrows none of its logic. The cheapest diagnostic: ask twenty recent customers, in their own words, what they believe they are paying for, and check whether their answer matches the unit the company actually bills.

Reporting gross transaction value as revenue in a marketplace or commission model. The symptom is a board deck or press narrative citing a “revenue” figure that bears no resemblance to what shows up in the bank statement or the audited profit-and-loss statement. The underlying misunderstanding is treating money that merely passes through the platform as though the platform earned all of it, rather than only its commission. The cheapest diagnostic: reconcile the headline revenue number to actual cash collected by the company, not cash that changed hands between the two parties the company merely connected.

Underestimating the cash-timing mismatch when shifting from a one-time to a recurring model. The symptom is a company whose annual-recurring-revenue chart looks healthy and climbing while its bank balance quietly tightens, sometimes to the point of a real cash crunch, in the middle of the transition. The underlying misunderstanding is that accounting revenue recognised on a subscription is collected in instalments and deferred over the period it covers, while a hardware sale’s cash and revenue land the same day — so a company that used to fund next quarter from this quarter’s hardware sales can find itself short even as its reported top line grows. The cheapest diagnostic: build an eighteen-month cash bridge alongside the ARR projection, not instead of it, and check whether the low point in that bridge is one the company can actually survive.

Bundling too many revenue streams before the company has the sales and billing muscle to sustain the complexity. The symptom is a sales cycle that keeps lengthening, and new sales hires who cannot explain the company’s pricing in a single sentence without consulting notes. The underlying misunderstanding is mistaking Amazon’s five-stream sophistication for a template to copy immediately, rather than a structure Amazon itself built one stream at a time over two decades. The cheapest diagnostic: time how long it takes a newly hired representative to explain the pricing correctly, unprompted, in under thirty seconds — if they cannot, customers cannot either.

8. What good looks like

Eighteen months before Meera’s board meeting, Arjun Mehta, product lead at Raagini Health, had faced a related version of the same decision and handled it in a way worth holding up as the target. Raagini Health’s marketplace, matching home-nurses to patients, earned its 18 percent commission cleanly on individual bookings, but Arjun noticed that a meaningful share of demand was coming from hospitals wanting standing, dedicated nursing staff rather than one-off bookings — a fundamentally different buyer, with a fundamentally different willingness to pay for predictability rather than for a single match. Rather than force that hospital demand through the same commission mechanism built for individual patients, Arjun built a second, deliberately separate revenue model alongside the first: a monthly subscription, priced per nurse retained, sold directly to hospital procurement teams on annual contracts. He resisted pressure to simply raise the commission rate on hospital bookings instead, which would have been faster to ship but would have priced Raagini Health out of exactly the segment it was trying to win, because hospitals wanted budget certainty, not a percentage that moved with volume they could not fully predict.

Within a year, the hospital subscription line, though it served a small fraction of Raagini Health’s total user base, contributed close to a third of total gross profit, because its margins were cleaner and its churn was lower than the transactional marketplace business it sat beside. What made the decision good was not the specific mechanism Arjun chose but the discipline behind choosing it: he identified that a different buyer needed a different unit of charge, built the arithmetic before pitching the change, and kept the two revenue models legible and separate rather than folding one clumsily into the other. That was the shape of the decision Meera was trying to bring to her own board.

9. What Meera decided

Meera walked into the board meeting with the 21 percent breakeven number, the 45 percent pilot-based attach-rate estimate that sat comfortably above it, and a recommendation: cut the ring’s price to ₹3,999, launch the subscription with a genuine sales push rather than leave it unmarketed inside the app, and treat attach rate — not device volume, not app downloads — as the single metric the leadership team would review weekly for the next two quarters. She paired the recommendation with the honest range: even a disappointing 20 percent attach rate left the business only marginally worse off than where it already stood, which meant the downside of trying was small and clearly bounded, while the upside — a ₹10.22 crore run-rate against Ratnika Circle’s Series C target — was not. The board approved the shift, with one condition Meera had already built into her own plan: an eighteen-month cash bridge, reviewed monthly, so a healthy ARR chart would never again be mistaken for a healthy bank balance.

What Meera would need to learn next follows directly from where this decision left off. Subscription economics — cohort retention curves, monthly churn, and lifetime value calculated properly rather than assumed — determines whether the 45 percent attach rate she pitched actually compounds into a durable business or decays within a year as novelty wears off. And the choice of value metric, the specific unit a subscription’s price scales with, will decide whether Ratnika Circle’s ₹499 flat fee is still the right number once the company tries to sell the coaching layer to serious athletes who use it daily and casual owners who barely open the app — two customers a flat fee treats identically today, but may not be able to serve identically tomorrow.

Two questions worth sitting with, beyond Ratnika Circle’s specific numbers.

First: if a competitor copies Ratnika Circle’s coaching content within a year — and coaching content is easier to copy than a physical product — does the subscription still create real lock-in, or does the company need a second, harder-to-copy reason for a subscriber to stay, such as a community, a coach relationship, or accumulated personal data the subscriber would lose by switching?

Second: a revenue-model transition always creates winners and losers inside the company before it creates them outside it. Whose incentives, whose quarterly numbers, and whose job security have to be deliberately protected during the eighteen months a company spends converting hardware margin into recurring revenue — and what happens to the model if that protection is never put in place?

Lokmitra: Choosing How to Get Paid

A decision case in revenue models

1. Opening

At 7:40 on Thursday morning, 22 October 2026, Vidula Ektare sat alone in Lokmitra's office in Kalyani Nagar, Pune, with two screens open. One held the results of an eight-week pricing pilot that had closed on Sunday. The other held the bank balance: ₹900 lakh at 30 September.

On Friday 30 October, at 4:00 pm IST, the board would meet. As chief product officer and co-founder, Vidula was to recommend how a company that gave its product away to most merchants should begin to earn from them. Her finance chief wanted a model that investors could see in the numbers before a Series A round planned for the first half of 2027. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, the busiest fortnight in a shopkeeper's year, and she also had to say whether the change should launch before it or after.

2. Company background

Lokmitra, founded in 2019, sells a billing and bookkeeping app, in seven Indian languages, to small shops. A merchant issues GST invoices, tracks stock and customer credit, and prints a UPI QR code on every bill. In September 2026, 3,20,000 merchants issued at least one invoice; Lokmitra calls these its active merchants.

The field is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit lead with free ledgers, Vyapar and Zoho Books sell paid plans, and PhonePe and Paytm hand shopkeepers a QR code and a soundbox. UPI payments to merchants carry no merchant discount rate, so Lokmitra earns nothing when a customer pays.

Annual operating cost is ₹720 lakh across 41 people in Pune, Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and New Jersey. Annual revenue is ₹132 lakh: ₹84 lakh from consumer-goods distributors who buy promoted-product slots on the invoice screen, and ₹48 lakh from Almas Gulf Distribution FZE, a Dubai wholesaler that licenses a white-labelled Lokmitra to its Indian distributors under a contract with a ₹48 lakh annual minimum through March 2028. Net burn is therefore ₹588 lakh a year, or ₹49 lakh a month.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows the merchants. About two in three invoice about ₹1 lakh a month; fewer than one in ten invoice around ₹20 lakh. Figure 1 sets out the calendar.

Three proposals reached Vidula within a fortnight. The first came from her own team. Between 24 August and 18 October, Lokmitra offered a paid tier to 4,000 merchants drawn in proportion to the base, at ₹150, ₹300 or ₹800 a month depending on segment; 272 paid. The second came from a Mumbai non-bank lender, which would pay Lokmitra 1.5 per cent of every working-capital loan it disbursed to a Lokmitra merchant, the lender underwriting and carrying each loan, with invoice history shared on the merchant's consent under the DPDP Act and the loan documented under the RBI's digital lending directions. The lender's underwriters supplied the take-up estimates in Exhibit 2. The third came from Vibhas Ekdalkar in New Jersey, whose pipeline of six wholesalers, cooperative banks and trade associations would each pay a yearly fee per retailer on a private-label Lokmitra; two have sent letters of intent.

The team sees it from where it sits. The data scientist in Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Pune until the clocks change on 1 November, notes that only the first monthly renewal fell inside the window, so two months of data say little about how long payers stay. The designer in Berlin has drawn a paywall that appears at a merchant's first invoice and worries about that first impression.

4. The people

Vidula Ektare, chief product officer and co-founder, Pune, must make the recommendation and wants a model that teaches the company something true about what merchants will pay for.

Vinayak Ekhande, chief financial officer, Mumbai, wants revenue that recurs, can be forecast by the quarter, and adds no balance-sheet risk before the Series A.

Vinita Enamdar, head of customer success, Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of Pune, runs the Gulf-hours support desk that Almas's contract requires, and takes merchants' calls in Marathi and Hindi. She wants the smallest shops' trust protected and the support queue kept manageable.

6. The options

Option A, subscription. Charge every merchant a monthly fee by segment, ₹150, ₹300 or ₹800, as piloted, with a free tier that keeps basic invoicing. It needs a paywall and entitlement build of ₹60 lakh and a larger support team. It leaves the promoted slots, the lender conversation and the Almas contract untouched, and it changes what every merchant sees on the invoice screen.

Option B, transaction. Place working-capital loans with the Mumbai lender for Small and Mid merchants and earn 1.5 per cent of each loan. Micro merchants stay free. It needs a consent flow, a data pipeline and a credit-operations team costing ₹150 lakh to build. Revenue arrives only when a merchant borrows. It leaves the invoice screen as it is.

Option C, licensing. Sign the six partners and sell each a private-label Lokmitra at ₹600 per retailer seat per year, while Lokmitra's own app stays free. It needs a multi-tenant build of ₹220 lakh and implementation and enterprise-sales staff. It leaves the merchants' own experience and the current promoted slots unchanged.

8. A note for the learner

A revenue model is the capture half of a business model: it fixes who pays, for what event, and how often. The options differ on all three. A merchant pays monthly under A, a borrowing merchant pays once per loan under B, and a partner pays yearly per seat under C. Because they charge different parties, they should be compared as steady-state annual contribution, as Exhibit 3 does, and then weighed by how well each volume is evidenced.

One defensible path is to recommend Option A as piloted, launching on Monday 16 November, after Diwali, so that the first paying month is an ordinary month rather than a festival one. The case for it is that its volume comes from Lokmitra's own merchants, its running cost falls between B's and C's, and it is the only option that exposes every segment to a price and so teaches the company what each is worth. At the stated volumes, A and B each exceed the ₹588 lakh annual net burn, while C, at ₹490 lakh, falls ₹98 lakh short.

The recommendation should carry its own stop condition: if fewer than 80 per cent of those who paid in the first week after launch have paid again by 31 December, pause the rollout and revisit B. Meanwhile, begin the lender's consent-flow design at low cost, and hold C until at least one letter of intent becomes a signed contract. Other paths are defensible; this one names the evidence behind each step and says what would end it.
